questions.title: How fat-soluble molecules enter a cell
questions.question: How do fat-soluble molecules normally get into a cell?

options.B: They pass through protein pores in the cell membrane
options.C: They dissolve in the fat layers of the membrane and enter the cell by diffusion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fat-soluble molecules do routinely cross the cell membrane; the question is by which route.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein pores/channels are the route for water-soluble ions and small polar molecules, not for fat-soluble ones, which do not need a protein channel to cross.
explanations.C: Correct. The cell membrane's core is a lipid bilayer, so a fat-soluble (lipid-soluble) molecule simply dissolves into that lipid core and diffuses across it down its own concentration gradient, without needing a protein carrier or channel. This route -- simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer -- is how lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, alcohols and steroid hormones normally cross cell membranes. This is a direct consequence of the membrane's basic phospholipid-bilayer architecture, which readily admits lipid-soluble molecules while excluding most water-soluble ones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is a bulk, vesicle-based uptake mechanism used for particles and large complexes, not the normal route for small fat-soluble molecules.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that fat-soluble molecules cross the cell membrane by dissolving in and diffusing through its lipid bilayer.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: They dissolve in the fat layers of the membrane and enter the cell by diffusion", p34

questions.title: What increases the rate of diffusion across a membrane
questions.question: The rate of diffusion of a particle across a membrane will increase if:

options.A: The size of the particle increases
options.B: The number of protein channels increases
options.D: The thickness of the membrane increases

explanations.A: Incorrect. A larger particle diffuses more slowly, not faster, since diffusion rate is inversely related to particle (molecular) size.
explanations.B: Correct. Facilitated diffusion of ions and polar molecules depends on the availability of protein channels (or carriers) in the membrane, so increasing the number of these channels increases the total cross-sectional pathway available for the particle to cross, raising the rate of diffusion. This is directly analogous to widening a doorway: more open channels mean more particles can cross per unit time for a given concentration gradient. This principle underlies physiological up- or down-regulation of channel/transporter number as a way of tuning membrane permeability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lower temperature slows molecular motion and so decreases, rather than increases, the rate of diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A thicker membrane increases the diffusion distance a particle must cross, which decreases, rather than increases, the rate of diffusion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an increased number of membrane protein channels as a factor that raises the rate of diffusion across the cell membrane.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The number of protein channels increases", p35
